newsitem.title: UK: Europeans don't trust biotechnology, study finds.
newsitem.headline: Europeans don't trust biotechnology, study finds.

text.p: Most Europeans do not trust their governments to protect them from the possible dangers of genetically modified food, researchers said on Wednesday.
A survey across the European Union showed most people want labelling on such products and are worried about the moral implications of genetically engineering animals.

"Many Europeans are uneasy about modern biotechnology, particularly about new genetic technologies," George Gaskell of the London School of Economics and an international team of researchers said in a commentary in the science journal Nature.
Gaskell's team used research companies to interview more than 16,000 people across the European Union in October and November 1996.
"There is a sense that issues of biotechnology are beyond the scope of national governments to regulate," he told a news conference. Even the European Parliament got few votes of confidence.
Consumers would rather see agencies like the World Health Organisation in charge, he said.
Most trusted sources of information are medical doctors and animal welfare groups, while the biotech companies are least trusted.

Britons, in particular, are concerned about morality, Gaskell added. "They ask, 'Is it any good? Is it morally acceptable?'" he said. "We see that as a different stance from that taken by regulators, which is 'is there any risk?'"

The European Commission earlier this month gave formal approval to compulsory labelling of all genetically modified farm products from July 31. Labels must specify products "may contain or consist of genetically modified organisms".

John Durant, assistant director of London's Science Museum and one of the coordinators of the study, said biomedical applications especially worried people -- and companies should take note. "They can't afford to take public opinon for granted," he said.
The survey found 74 percent of those interviewed wanted genetically modified food to be labelled.
Only 28 percent thought regulation should be left to the industry, while 60 percent thought only traditional breeding methods should be used for farm animals.

Earlier this year, street protests broke out in several European cities after governments approved the import of soybeans that had been genetically modified by Monsanto Co to resist one of its herbicides.
U.S. exporters and industry said it would be impossible to label the soybeans or products, ranging from cooking oil to bread, that contained them.
The survey was done before the announcement in March that scientists had cloned an adult sheep. "It would be nice to know what the effect of Dolly has been," Duncan said.
The survey also found 53 percent of people thought current regulations were not enough to protect them from any dangers. Some critics say transgenic plants could cause allergies or even disease.
Gaskell said there were strong indications that people did not understand the science involved. Images of Frankenstein and eugenics were frequently invoked, he said.
"We heard some strange things. People thought that, for example, ordinary tomatoes didn't have genes in and the whole process of genetic engineering was adding a gene in."

But there was a real belief that genetic engineering was unnecessary. "People say...'Things don't taste that bad anyway'," Gaskell said. "People aren't persuaded that this is in their interest while they recognise that it is in the producers' interest."
Dennis Purcell, Managing Director for Life Sciences for investment bankers Hambrecht and Quist, said he was not concerned about potential effects on biotech companies.
"I think the United States went through the same process 10 years ago when there were a lot of questions in people's minds about what biotechnology was," he said.
Lobbying could help educate, he said.
"One thing we don't have in Europe yet is a unified party speaking on behalf of the sector."
